title: Analytical mechanics
tagline: Coordinates chosen for the problem, not for the axes
summary: Constraints and generalised coordinates, Lagrange’s equations, central-force motion, rigid bodies, small oscillations, Hamilton’s equations and a first look at chaos.
overview: Newtonian mechanics in Cartesian coordinates becomes painful as soon as a constraint removes a degree of freedom: a bead on a wire, a pendulum, a rolling disc. Lagrange’s method takes the constraints as the definition of the coordinates, writes the kinetic and potential energy, and produces the equations of motion without a catalogue of constraint forces.

After the calculus of variations and Lagrange’s equations, the course treats the two classical applications that justify the machinery: motion under a central force, including Kepler’s problem, and the free rotation of a rigid body. Small oscillations about equilibrium are a systematic version of the normal modes already met for springs. Hamilton’s equations and canonical transformations restate the same theory in phase space, which is the language of statistical mechanics and of quantum mechanics. A final chapter shows what a nonlinear system can do that a linear one cannot.

The skill being taught is the choice of coordinate. A good generalised coordinate is one whose kinetic energy you can write down, and whose constraint is already built in. If you cannot write T and V, no formalism will help.
outcomes: Count degrees of freedom, classify constraints as holonomic or nonholonomic, and choose generalised coordinates that build the constraints in.
Derive Lagrange’s equations from d’Alembert’s principle and from Hamilton’s principle of stationary action, and use them with generalised forces and Lagrange multipliers.
Prove Noether’s theorem and use symmetries of the Lagrangian to find conserved momenta and the conserved energy function.
Reduce the two-body central-force problem to an effective one-dimensional problem, derive Kepler’s three laws, and compute orbits and Rutherford scattering angles.
Compute inertia tensors and principal axes, derive Euler’s equations, and explain torque-free precession and the instability of rotation about the intermediate axis.
Find the normal modes and frequencies of a coupled system from its mass and stiffness matrices, by hand and numerically.
Construct the Hamiltonian by a Legendre transformation, use Hamilton’s equations and Poisson brackets, check canonical transformations, and prove Liouville’s theorem.
Analyse fixed points of nonlinear systems, read Poincaré sections, and compute Lyapunov exponents for the driven damped pendulum and the logistic map.

chapters.title: Constraints and virtual work

chapters.title: Lagrange’s equations
chapters.summary: The calculus of variations, Hamilton’s principle, cyclic coordinates and Noether’s theorem.

chapters.title: Central forces
chapters.summary: Reduction to one body, the effective potential, Kepler orbits, Bertrand’s theorem and Rutherford scattering.

chapters.title: Rigid-body dynamics
chapters.summary: The inertia tensor, principal axes, Euler’s equations, torque-free precession and the tennis-racket instability.

chapters.title: Small oscillations
chapters.summary: Equilibria, the mass and stiffness matrices, the generalised eigenproblem, normal modes and their numerical computation.

history.title: D’Alembert’s principle
history.detail: In the Traité de dynamique, Jean le Rond d’Alembert reduced dynamics to statics by requiring the “lost forces” to be in equilibrium under the constraints, which eliminates the constraint forces.

history.title: Euler’s rigid-body dynamics
history.detail: Euler’s Theoria motus corporum solidorum seu rigidorum set out principal axes and the equations of rotation now named after him, which he had derived in Berlin memoirs of the 1750s.

history.title: Mécanique analytique
history.detail: Lagrange’s treatise, famously without a single figure, derived all of mechanics from the principle of virtual work in arbitrary coordinates, with multipliers for constraints and a general theory of small oscillations.

history.title: Hamilton’s general method in dynamics
history.detail: Hamilton’s two essays in the Philosophical Transactions of 1834 and 1835 stated the principle of stationary action with fixed end times and introduced the canonical equations and the principal function.

history.title: Liouville’s theorem
history.detail: Joseph Liouville proved the result on solutions of differential equations that implies the conservation of phase-space volume under Hamiltonian flow, later the foundation of statistical mechanics.

history.title: Jacobi’s lectures on dynamics
history.detail: Jacobi’s Königsberg lectures of 1842–43, published in 1866, developed canonical transformations and the Hamilton–Jacobi method of solving problems through a complete integral.

history.title: Poincaré and the three-body problem
history.detail: In his corrected prize memoir in Acta Mathematica, Poincaré showed that the three-body problem has orbits of tangled complexity and lacks the analytic integrals hoped for, the beginning of the modern study of chaos.

history.title: Noether’s theorem
history.detail: In “Invariante Variationsprobleme”, Emmy Noether proved that every continuous symmetry of an action gives a conservation law, for mechanics and for field theories alike.

history.title: Deterministic nonperiodic flow
history.detail: Edward Lorenz showed that three simple equations for convection have bounded solutions that never repeat and depend sensitively on initial conditions; the KAM theorem on the survival of invariant tori was completed in the same years.

history.title: Feigenbaum’s universal constant
history.detail: Mitchell Feigenbaum published the discovery that period-doubling cascades in all single-humped maps share the ratio δ = 4.6692…, later observed in convection, electronic circuits and lasers.

references.title: Classical Mechanics
references.note: The best first book on Lagrangians: clear, careful and full of worked examples. Chapters 6–13 cover this course, and Chapter 12 is an excellent numerical introduction to the driven damped pendulum.

references.title: Classical Dynamics of Particles and Systems
references.authors: Stephen T. Thornton and Jerry B. Marion
references.note: Fifth edition. A standard intermediate text with many problems on central forces, rigid bodies and coupled oscillations.

references.title: Classical Mechanics
references.authors: Herbert Goldstein, Charles Poole and John Safko
references.note: Third edition. The traditional graduate text: rigid bodies, canonical transformations, Hamilton–Jacobi theory, and a proof of Bertrand’s theorem in an appendix.

references.title: Mechanics
references.authors: L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz
references.note: Third edition. Short, deep and opinionated; derives everything from symmetry and the action. Read it after Taylor, not before.

references.title: Classical Dynamics: A Contemporary Approach
references.authors: Jorge V. José and Eugene J. Saletan
references.note: A modern geometric treatment that connects Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics to manifolds, symplectic structure, perturbation theory and chaos.

references.title: Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
references.note: Second edition. The standard introduction to fixed points, bifurcations, the logistic map, Feigenbaum universality and the Lorenz equations, with physical applications throughout.

references.title: Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics
references.note: Second edition. The mathematician’s classic: symplectic geometry, Liouville’s theorem, action–angle variables and an overview of the KAM theorem.
